patterns.title: Rule Beating
patterns.domain: Systems and feedback traps; adaptive evasion of operational boundaries, formal compliance, rule design, and incentives

sources.author: Donella H. Meadows
sources.title: Thinking in Systems: A Primer
sources.read_method: Opened and read the Rule Beating section, printed pages 136–137 (PDF pages 152–153), and the adjacent discussion distinguishing rule beating from seeking the wrong goal.
sources.supports: Named systems trap of evasive adaptation around rules; formal compliance versus purpose; redesigning rules so that ingenuity supports the intended outcome.
sources.boundary: Foundational systems synthesis, not a formal theorem or controlled estimate of any proposed enforcement intervention. The article does not claim Meadows invented all prior analysis of gaming or distorted incentives. Historical examples in the book are not imported as independently verified cases.

sources.author: Steven Kerr
sources.title: On the Folly of Rewarding A, While Hoping for B
sources.read_method: Opened original scanned-paper mirror, whose searchable text was unavailable, then opened and read the original-text transcription, including the introduction on rewarded versus hoped-for behavior and official versus operative goals. Journal record identifies Academy of Management Journal 18(4), 769–783.
sources.supports: Earlier analysis of reward arrangements that promote conduct inconsistent with stated purposes. Used as broader intellectual context, not attribution of the named Rule Beating trap.
sources.boundary: Conceptual and illustrative source. No dated medical, military, or organizational examples are carried into the article as verified empirical findings.

sources.author: Gwyn Bevan and Christopher Hood
sources.title: What’s Measured Is What Matters: Targets and Gaming in the English Public Health Care System
sources.read_method: Opened full primary paper and read introduction and analysis of gaming/audit limitations, especially printed pages 529–535 (PDF pages 12–18).
sources.supports: Reported practices shifting patients across the emergency-department measurement boundary; uncertainty about the extent of gaming and genuine improvement under fragmentary audit.
sources.boundary: Analysis synthesizing inquiries, reports, surveys, and studies, not a randomized intervention or complete audit of providers. The historical ambulance example is reported practice rather than a quantified general prevalence estimate. Some documented gaming elsewhere involved falsification; lawful formal compliance and deception are not equated.

sources.title: US Federal Acquisition Regulation, 13.003(c)(2)
sources.supports: Official text expressly addresses splitting aggregated requirements into purchases below applicable thresholds to avoid procedures or requirements.
sources.boundary: Specific published procurement rule; no thresholds reproduced and no assertion that this fictional software or every organization follows that regime. No general legal advice or claim that passing a narrow test establishes legality.
sources.read_method: Opened official section and read paragraph (c)(2), including both listed purposes of prohibited splitting.

patterns.short_description: Identify how an operational rule can be satisfied while its purpose is defeated, then redesign the relevant boundary, incentives, and review process without merely multiplying restrictions.
use_when: Which larger requirement should the review actually govern?
goals: Recognize the familiar situation and preserve the defining mechanism.
Distinguish formal assumptions, empirical findings, and hypothetical continuations.
Make intervention authority, opportunity costs, and remaining constraints explicit.
mechanisms: Review the related overall requirement, with proportionate linkage and a legitimate exception route.
Genuine separate needs must not be merged arbitrarily. Review costs time; complete rules may already prohibit splitting.

example_structure.scenario: One known planned acquisition is fragmented into requests passing a fictional narrow amount check. Apparent test compliance is explicitly separated from full policy compliance; genuine separate needs or permitted staging may differ. Linking the aggregate requirement restores review, not automatic refusal or budget. Identity/aggregation evidence, explanation, appeals, urgency, review cost, and changed authority matter. FAR anti-splitting text is a source-specific counterpart, not a claim about all regimes.
example_structure.changed_relationship: Review the related overall requirement, with proportionate linkage and a legitimate exception route.
example_structure.residual_constraints: Genuine separate needs must not be merged arbitrarily. Review costs time; complete rules may already prohibit splitting.
example_structure.comparison: Qualitative choices, dependencies, and consequences; no invented scores, computed trajectory, or measured improvement claimed.

visual.question: Which larger requirement should the review actually govern?
visual.alternative_text: Hypothetical qualitative illustration. Related small requests for one planned purchase each pass a narrow amount check. The enclosing boundary shows their shared requirement. Linking that requirement and reviewing its total changes what is checked, with explanation and appeal for mistaken grouping. Change: Review the related overall requirement, with proportionate linkage and a legitimate exception route. Limitation: Genuine separate needs must not be merged arbitrarily. Review costs time; complete rules may already prohibit splitting.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. The records pass the fictional per-request test while the overall commitment escapes review. That is not proof of full policy compliance. Aggregate review can restore scrutiny while imposing delay, reducing scope, or rejecting the plan; it creates no extra budget.
